text: Tonya Maxene Price, born November 12, 1970, in Portland, Oregon, is an American former figure skater, boxer, and reality television personality. She was raised in East Portland by her mother, LaVona Golden (born 1940), and father, Albert Harding (1933–2009), who held various odd jobs and was often underemployed due to poor health. Harding began ice skating at age three with coach Diane Rawlinson and also learned hunting, drag racing, and auto mechanics from her father. LaVona struggled to support the family, hand-sewing her daughter’s skating costumes to save money, and the couple divorced after 19 years in 1987 when Harding was 16. She dropped out of Milwaukie High School during her sophomore year to focus on skating and earned a GED in 1988. Harding claimed she suffered frequent physical and psychological abuse from her mother, with LaVona admitting to one instance of hitting her at an ice rink. In her 2008 biography, The Tonya Tapes, she stated she was the victim of acquaintance rape in 1991 and that her half-brother, Chris Davison, molested her as a child; she reported the abuse in 1986, and Davison was briefly imprisoned before being killed in an unsolved hit-and-run in 1988. She later said Davison was the only person in her life she hated and unworthy of forgiveness. Harding trained with Rawlinson through the mid-1980s, placing sixth in 1986, fifth in 1987 and 1988, and third in 1989. After the 1989 Nationals, she trained with Dody Teachman and won Skate America in October 1989. In 1991, she completed her first triple Axel in competition on February 16, becoming the first American woman to do so and the second woman in history (after Midori Ito) to land it internationally. She won the 1991 U.S. Ladies' Singles title with the event’s first 6.0 technical merit score since Janet Lynn’s 1973 performance and finished second at the March 1991 World Championships behind Kristi Yamaguchi and ahead of Nancy Kerrigan, marking the first time one country swept the ladies’ medal podium. At the September 1991 Skate America, she recorded three more firsts. Despite these achievements, she never successfully completed the triple Axel again after 1991, and her results declined. She placed third at the January 1992 U.S. Championships despite a twisted ankle and finished fourth at the February 1992 Winter Olympics. On March 1, 1992, she dismissed Teachman and returned to Rawlinson. She placed sixth at the 1992 World Championships and fourth at the November 1992 Skate Canada International. In the 1993 season, she skated poorly at the U.S. Championships and failed to qualify for the World team. In January 1994, she won the U.S. Championships but was later stripped of the title when the USFSA voted to vacate it in June 1994 following an investigation into the attack on Nancy Kerrigan. Despite the controversy, she remained on the U.S. Olympic team for the 1994 Winter Olympics in Lillehammer. After a broken skate lace in her long program, she was given a re-skate and finished eighth, behind Oksana Baiul (gold) and Nancy Kerrigan (silver). On January 6, 1994, one day before the U.S. Championships, Kerrigan was attacked in a corridor at the Detroit Cobo Arena by Shane Stant, who used a 21-inch ASP telescopic baton to strike her right leg above the knee. Stant, hired by Harding’s ex-husband Jeff Gillooly and bodyguard Shawn Eckardt, turned himself in on January 14. The attack was intended to prevent Kerrigan from competing in the Nationals or Olympics. On January 11, Harding was interviewed by KOIN-TV, where she said, “I have definitely thought about it,” with Gillooly standing behind her. She confirmed speaking with FBI agents in Detroit and Portland. On January 13, Eckardt and Smith were arrested. On January 16, Harding’s lawyer held a press conference denying her involvement. On January 18, she submitted to over ten hours of questioning by the DA and FBI, during which she admitted knowing of the plot after the fact, settling on a cover story with Gillooly and Eckardt on January 10, witnessing pay phone calls to Smith on January 10 and 11, and lying to FBI agents on January 18. In the transcript, she stated, “I hope everyone understands. I'm telling on someone I really care about. I know now [Jeff] is involved. I'm sorry.” On January 19, Gillooly surrendered to the FBI. On January 20, Diane Sawyer asked Harding on Primetime whether she had done anything wrong; she said she had not. On January 27, Gillooly testified, possibly implicating Harding, and her friend Stephanie Quintero said Harding was shocked and hurt, believing in Jeff. On February 1, 1994, Gillooly’s attorney negotiated a plea bargain, resulting in Gillooly and Eckardt pleading guilty to racketeering, Stant and Smith to conspiracy to commit second-degree assault, and Gillooly sentenced to two years in prison and publicly apologizing to Kerrigan, calling the apology “hollow.” Judge Donald Londer noted the attack could have injured Kerrigan more seriously. Eckardt died in 2007. On February 1, the USFSA disciplinary panel found reasonable grounds to believe Harding violated the sport’s code of ethics due to her failure to report the assault, leading to a formal charge of making false statements about her knowledge. Claire Ferguson, USFSA president, decided not to suspend Harding before a hearing. The panel reviewed testimonies from Stant and Smith, telephone records, and notes found in a Portland saloon trash bin. Harding was given 30 days to respond. News media attended her practices and filmed her barefoot running to stop a tow truck on February 7. On February 10, Connie Chung interviewed her, saying, “I never did anything to hurt [Jeff]. If I ever did anything, it was to stick up for him and protect him.” Chung also flew with Harding to Oslo on February 15. On February 17, Harding and Kerrigan practiced together at the Hamar Olympic Amphitheatre, with approximately 400 press members present; Kerrigan wore the same costume as during the attack, which she later said was deliberate and empowering. The February 23 technical program broadcast was one of the most-watched telecasts in the U.S. On February 25, Harding finished eighth after a bootlace broke early in her free skate, and she was allowed a re-skate. Kerrigan won silver behind Oksana Baiul. On March 9, 1994, Judge Owen Panner granted Harding a stay until June on her disciplinary hearing. Portland authorities stated the criminal investigation would conclude by March 21. On March 16, 1994, Harding pled guilty to conspiracy to hinder prosecution as a Class C felony, negotiating a plea bargain with her lawyer Robert Weaver to avoid further prosecution. Judge Donald Londer confirmed she entered the plea knowingly and voluntarily. Her plea admissions included knowing of the assault plot after the fact, settling on a cover story with Gillooly and Eckardt on January 10, witnessing pay phone calls to Smith on January 10 and 11, and lying to FBI agents on January 18. The attack received widespread media coverage, appearing on the covers of Sports Illustrated, Newsweek, and Time. Abby Haight and J.E. Vader wrote a biography of Harding called Fire on Ice, including excerpts from her January 18 FBI interview. Harding later competed professionally from 2003 to 2004, placing second at the ESPN Pro Skating Championship in 1999. Her life has been the subject of numerous books, films, documentaries, and academic studies. In 2014, two documentaries, Nancy & Tonya and The Price of Gold, were released, inspiring Steven Rogers to write the film I, Tonya in 2017, in which Margot Robbie portrayed Harding. In 2018, she was a contestant on season 26 of Dancing with the Stars, finishing third, and in 2019, she won season 16 of Worst Cooks in America. The United States Figure Skating Association banned her for life on June 30, 1994, after her involvement in covering up the assault.

Nancy Kerrigan, after recovering from her injury, won a silver medal behind Oksana Baiul from Ukraine. On March 9, 1994, Judge Owen Panner granted Harding a stay until June on her disciplinary hearing. Portland authorities stated the criminal investigation would conclude by March 21, with any indictments and a grand jury report to be issued at that time. On March 16, 1994, Harding pled guilty to conspiracy to hinder prosecution as a Class C felony offense at a Multnomah County court hearing, with her lawyer Robert Weaver negotiating a plea bargain that ensured no further prosecution. Judge Donald Londer confirmed Harding entered her plea knowingly and voluntarily. Her admissions included knowing of the assault plot after the fact, settling on a cover story with Gillooly and Eckardt on January 10, witnessing pay phone calls to Smith affirming the story on January 10 and 11, and lying to the FBI with the story on January 18. Law enforcement had been following and videotaping the co-conspirators since January 10. Her penalties were three years of probation, a $100,000 fine, 500 hours of community service, reimbursement of $10,000 in legal expenses to Multnomah County, a psychiatric examination, and a $50,000 donation to Special Olympics Oregon (SOOR). Oregon sentencing guidelines carried a maximum penalty of five years in prison. The plea agreement required Harding to resign from the U.S. Figure Skating Association, forcing her withdrawal from the 1994 Worlds (scheduled for March 17). District Attorney Norman Frink stated that if Harding had not agreed to the plea, she would have faced an indictment on all possible charges and punishment including loss of skating privileges. Phil Knight, CEO of Nike, donated $25,000 toward Harding's legal fees, and she had earned approximately $600,000 from an Inside Edition deal. Weaver said the plea agreement was satisfactory because it avoided prison, stating "We would have prevailed at trial." A USFSA executive commented that they did not know if Harding was innocent or guilty, if she was involved before the national championship. On March 18, Claire Ferguson decided the disciplinary hearing would proceed in June. The USFSA executive committee discussed Harding's reinstatement and whether to strip her of the 1994 National Championship title, but no decision was made. On March 21, 1994, a Portland grand jury issued an indictment stating there was evidence Harding participated in the attack plot, based on more than two months of investigation and testimonies from Diane Rawlinson, choreographer Erika Bakacs, writer Vera Marano, and Eckardt's college instructor and classmates. The indictment stated there was evidence Harding fraudulently used USFSA-provided skating monies to finance the assault and that Harding, Gillooly, Eckardt, Smith, and Stant agreed to "knowingly cause physical injury ... by means of a dangerous weapon," implying she was involved from the beginning or very closely. She was not charged due to the terms of her March 16 plea agreement. On June 29, 1994, the USFSA disciplinary panel met for nine hours over two days to consider Harding's alleged role in the attack. On June 30, chairman William Hybl stated that the panel found the FBI reports, court documents, and Harding's March 16 plea agreement presented sufficient evidence. Harding did not attend or participate in the hearing. Weaver said the decision disappointed her but was not surprising, and that she had not decided on an appeal. Harding was stripped of her 1994 U.S. Championship title and banned for life from USFSA events as a skater or coach. The USFSA has no authority over professional skating, but after the scandal, Harding became persona non grata on the pro circuit, with few skaters or promoters working with her and she did not benefit from the subsequent rise in professional skating. Shortly before the 1998 Winter Olympics, CBS and Fox aired two televised special reports on the scandal. Harry Smith hosted the CBS special, where Harding reiterated her January 27, 1994 statement: "I had no prior knowledge of the planned assault on Nancy Kerrigan." Smith then interviewed Kerrigan, who, after reviewing transcripts from Harding's January 18, 1994 FBI interview, concluded that "[Tonya] knew more than she admits." The Fox special, titled Breaking the Ice: The Women of '94 Revisited, hosted by James Brown, featured interviews with Harding, Gillooly, and Kerrigan. Gillooly (later renamed Jeff Stone in 1995) said Harding avoiding prison did not anger him and that he felt his own punishment was just. Stone reflected on Harding's "limited involvement" and speculated a "guilty conscience" still troubled her. Brown mediated a joint interview between Kerrigan and Harding, where both expressed sincere desires for happy families and well-wishes. Kerrigan said she hoped Harding could learn from her mistakes and "find happiness," and Harding said she was grateful to personally express remorse to Kerrigan. In her 2008 biography, The Tonya Tapes (transcribed by Lynda D. Prouse), Harding stated she wanted to call the FBI in 1994 to reveal what she knew but decided not to when Gillooly allegedly threatened her with death after a gunpoint gang rape by him and two other men she did not know. Gillooly responded with surprise that "groundless claims" against him could be published and claimed her gang rape accusation was "utterly ridiculous." In 2013, Deadspin sought Gillooly for an interview, and he again defended himself, expressing regret that Harding is often remembered for what he said she did, meaning allegedly plotting to injure Kerrigan. He admitted his past "stupidity" contributed to her 1994 downfall and maintained she was a great figure skater, saying, "I've had it easy, compared to poor Tonya... she tends to be the butt of the joke. It's kind of sad to me." In 2014, Nancy Kerrigan addressed the scandal in a brief interview with Bob Costas, stating, "Whatever apology Tonya has given, I accept it. It's time for all us—I've always wished [Tonya] well. She has her own family, I have my family. It's time to make that our focus, and move on with our lives." On February 15, 1994, an explicit 1991 videotape clip of Harding topless was shown on A Current Affair; three still frames were published in The Sun (a British tabloid). The New York Post reported that Gillooly supplied the videotape for an undisclosed sum. On June 22, 1994, in Portland, Oregon, Harding appeared on an AAA professional wrestling show as the manager for Los Gringos Locos, which included Art Barr and Eddie Guerrero. A promotional musical event in 1995 in Portland was unsuccessful when Harding and her band, the Golden Blades, were booed off stage. On July 26, 1994, Penthouse announced its September issue would feature stills of Harding and Gillooly having sex from the same extended videotape, which was copied and marketed exclusively by Penthouse. Both used the same agent to negotiate equal payment. In 1994, Harding was cast in Breakaway, an action film with Teri Fruichantie and Joseph "Joe" Estévez, centered on her being unwittingly involved in an organized crime syndicate's attempt to recover $300,000 of stolen money, released in 1996. Harding appeared on television on The Weakest Link: "15 Minutes of Fame Edition" in 2002 with Kato Kaelin, and in March 2008 became a commentator for TruTV's truTV Presents: World's Dumbest. Since leaving skating and boxing, Harding has worked as a welder, a painter at a metal fabrication company, and a hardware sales clerk at Sears. In 2017, she stated she worked as a painter and deck builder. She lives in Vancouver, Washington. In August 2019, Harding appeared in a U.S. television commercial promoting Direct Auto Insurance. In 2002, Harding boxed against Paula Jones on the Fox Network Celebrity Boxing event, winning the fight. On February 22, 2003, she made her official women's professional boxing debut, losing a four-round split decision against Samantha Browning on the undercard of Mike Tyson vs. Clifford Etienne. Her boxing career began amid rumors of financial difficulties and needed fighting to earn money. She fought on The Man Show and won against co-host Doug Stanhope, who later claimed on his podcast the fight was fixed because Harding refused to "fight a man." On March 23, 2004, she canceled a planned boxing match against Tracy Carlton in Oakland, California, due to an alleged death threat. On June 24, 2004, she was defeated by Amy Johnson in a match in Edmonton, Alberta, with fans booing her as she entered the ring and cheering for Johnson when she won in the third round. Her boxing career was cut short by asthma, with an overall record of three wins and three losses. On August 12, 2009, Harding set a new land speed record for a vintage gas coupe at 97.177 mph (156.391 km/h; 43.442 m/s) driving a 1931 Ford Model A named Lickity-Split on the Bonneville Salt Flats. On April 13, 2018, Harding was announced as one of the celebrities competing on season 26 of Dancing with the Stars, with professional partner Sasha Farber, finishing in third place. In August 2018, she was announced as one of the celebrities competing in the fifth celebrity edition of Food Network's Worst Cooks in America, set to broadcast in April 2019. Learning under Chef Anne Burrell, Harding ultimately won the competition, with the $25,000 prize going to St. Jude Children's Research Hospital. Harding is the only child of Albert Gordon Harding and LaVona Golden, who had been married three times and had four other children. The two divorced in 1987. Harding had a tumultuous relationship with her mother, alleging both physical and emotional abuse, including one incident where her mother threw a knife at her. LaVona denied the incident and claimed her daughter has a history of dishonesty. Harding began a relationship with 17-year-old Jeff Gillooly in September 1986 when she was 15. They moved into a home together in 1988 when he worked at the Oregon Liquor Control Commission. They married on March 18, 1990, when she was 19 and he was 22. In January 1992, Harding told Terry Richard of The Oregonian, "Jeff always put food on the table and a roof over my head. He paid for my skating for a couple of years. If it hadn't been for him during that time, I wouldn't have been skating." They divorced on August 28, 1993. During autumn 1993, Gillooly worked part-time managing Harding's career and took real estate classes. Harding and Gillooly continued seeing each other from early October 1993 until January 18, 1994, sharing a rented chalet in Beavercreek, Oregon. Harding married Michael Smith in 1995; they divorced in 1996. On October 29, 1996, Harding received media attention after using mouth-to-mouth resuscitation to revive an 81-year-old woman who collapsed at a bar in Portland while playing video poker. On February 22, 2000, Harding attacked her then-boyfriend Darren Silver, punching him repeatedly and throwing a hubcap at his head, leaving him with a bloodied face. She was arrested and initially pleaded not guilty to misdemeanor charges; in a May trial in Clark County District Court, she admitted to the attack and was sentenced to three days in jail, 10 days of community service, and a suspended jail sentence of 167 days. She married 42-year-old Joseph Price on June 23, 2010, when she was 39, and gave birth to a son named Gordon on February 19, 2011. On February 26, 2018, Harding stated on The Ellen DeGeneres Show that she is still active in skating and practices three times a week, performing several jumps and spins with her former coach Dody Teachman. Her life, career, and role in the 1994 attack have been widely referenced in popular culture, including a 2007 primary campaign speech by Barack Obama, in which he said, "Folks said there's no way Obama has a chance unless he goes and kneecaps the person ahead of us, does a Tonya Harding." In 2014, Matt Harkins and Viviana Olen created the Nancy Kerrigan and Tonya Harding Museum in their Brooklyn apartment, collecting and archiving memorabilia related to both. A contemporaneous Vogue article noted that Harding had developed a "cult following" over the years. In 1995, the book Women on Ice: Feminist Essays on the Tonya Harding/Nancy Kerrigan Spectacle was published, containing essays analyzing Harding's public image. Abigail Feder wrote that there existed "overdetermined femininity in Ladies' Figure Skating...femininity and athleticism are mutually exclusive concepts in American culture." Sam Stoloff wrote that during the scandal, the media emphasized Harding's class over her gender, subjecting her to a "litany of vaguely pejorative or mocking expressions" associated with "low class" cultural attributes, sometimes due to her personal interests. Stoloff theorized that Harding represented an American social class requiring interpretation ("the class Other") as referenced in Susan Orlean's 1994 essay "Figures in a Mall" in The New Yorker. In Sarah Marshall's 2014 essay "Remote Control: Tonya Harding, Nancy Kerrigan, and the Spectacles of Female Power and Pain," she noted the media's pervasive role in the 1994 scandal: "Somehow, in the scandal's aftermath, the form of the Tonya-bash was able to alchemize even the most chilling details of Tonya's life into tabloid gold." Marshall also examined Harding's "tomboy" persona in the context of figure skating, theorizing that she was rejected by the figure skating ethos because she did not conform to appearing as "beautiful without being sexual, strong without being intimidating, and vulnerable without being weak."

In her 2014 essay titled "Remote Control: Tonya Harding, Nancy Kerrigan, and the Spectacles of Female Power and Pain," writer Sarah Marshall highlighted the media's significant influence during the 1994 scandal, stating that "somehow, in the scandal's aftermath, the form of the Tonya-bash was able to alchemize even the most chilling details of Tonya's life into tabloid gold." Marshall also explored how Tonya Harding's "tomboy" image played a role in the figure skating world, arguing that she was rejected by the figure skating culture because she did not conform—according to Marshall's view, as many figure skaters including Nancy Kerrigan did—to the ideal of appearing "beautiful without being sexual, strong without being intimidating, and vulnerable without being weak."
